statements.claim: It was the month of Kartika under the star Revati; autumn had gone and the season of dew had come, and the earth around Upaplavya lay covered with abundant crops.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'The month was (Kaumuda Kartika) under the constellation Revati. It was the season of dew, Autumn having departed. The earth was covered with abundant crops all around.'

statements.claim: The night had passed and a bright sun rose in the east on the morning Krishna set out.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'The night having passed away, a bright sun arose in the east. The hour called Maitra set in, and the rays of the sun were still mild.'

statements.claim: Krishna had promised to ride to Hastinapura and ask for peace; Arjuna had begged him to go, and Krishna gave his word to the Kurus that he would come.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: Arjuna's plea to bring about peace and Krishna's reply, 'Yes, I will go to king Dhritarashtra, desirous of accomplishing what is consistent with righteousness...'

statements.claim: 'For months the Pandavas had lived on borrowed hope, and all of that hope now rested on a single journey.'
statements.evidence: Non-factual emotional framing of the stakes of the peace mission; no specific sourceable event asserted.

statements.claim: Before the sun was high Krishna finished his morning rites: bathed and anointed, he worshipped both the Sun and Fire, touched the tail of a bull, bowed to the brahmanas, walked round the sacred fire, and cast his eyes on the auspicious articles.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'purified himself by a bath, and decked his person with unguents and ornaments, worshipped both the Sun and Fire... touched the tail of a bull and reverently bowed to the Brahmanas, walked round the sacred fire, and cast his eyes on the (usual) auspicious articles placed in view.'

statements.claim: Krishna remembered Yudhishthira's request and called to Satyaki, Sini's grandson, who sat near him, ordering his car made ready with conch, discus, mace, quivers, darts and all weapons, because Duryodhana, Karna and Suvala's son are wicked-souled and even a contemptible foe should not be disregarded.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'Janardana recollected Yudhishthira's word and addressed Sini's grandson Satyaki, seated near, saying, "Let my car be made ready..."' — speech quoted near-verbatim.

statements.claim: His attendants understood the wishes of Kesava and yoked the marvellous car: wheels like the sun and moon, emblazoned with crescent and full moons, fishes, beasts and birds, garlands of flowers, pearls and gems, gold, a flagstaff with bright pennons, tiger-skins; the sight raised the hearts of the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083 detailed description of the car ('two wheels that resembled the sun and the moon... emblazonments of moons... fishes, animals, and birds... garlands of diverse flowers... pearls and gems... variegated with gems and gold... flag-staff bearing beautiful pennons... covered with tiger-skins... enhanced the joy of the Yadavas').

statements.claim: The four great horses Saivya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa and Valahaka, bathed and in beautiful harness, were yoked to the car.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'they yoked unto it those excellent steeds named Saivya and Sugriva and Meghapushpa and Valahaka, after these had been bathed and attired in beautiful harness.'

statements.claim: Garuda, lord of winged creatures, came down and perched on the flagstaff, making it rattle terribly; Krishna mounted the chariot high as the summit of Meru, its sound deep as a kettle-drum and loud as thunder, took Satyaki up, and set out filling the earth and sky with the rattle of his wheels.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'Garuda, the lord of the feathery creation, came and perched on the flag-staff of that car producing a terrible rattle... Saurin then mounted on that car, high as the summit of the Meru... And taking Satyaki also upon it, that best of male beings set out, filling the earth and the welkin with the rattle of his chariot-wheels.'

statements.claim: The sky became cloudless, auspicious winds blew, the air freed of dust grew pure; auspicious beasts and birds wheeled on his right, cranes, peacocks and swans cried good omens, and the altar fire blazed up toward the right free of smoke.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'the sky became cloudless, and auspicious winds began to blow around... auspicious animals and birds, whirling by the right side, began to follow him, and cranes and peacocks and swans all followed the slayer of Madhu, uttering cries of good omens. The very fire... freed from smoke blazed up cheerfully, sending forth its flames towards the right.'

statements.claim: On Krishna's right side stood the great sages Vasishtha, Vamadeva, Bhuridyumna, Gaya, Kratha, Sukra, Kusika and Bhrigu with other brahmarishis and celestial rishis.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'Vasishtha and Vamadeva, and Bhuridyumna and Gaya, and Kratha and Sukra and Kusika and Bhrigu, and other Brahmarshis and celestial Rishis... all stood on the right side of Krishna.'

statements.claim: Behind the chariot came the Pandavas — Yudhishthira son of Kunti, Bhima, Arjuna, the twin sons of Madri — with Chekitana, Dhrishtaketu ruler of the Chedis, Drupada, the king of Kasi and the mighty car-warrior Sikhandin.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, followed him, as also Bhima and Arjuna and those other Pandavas, viz., the twin sons of Madri. And the valiant Chekitana and Dhrishtaketu, the ruler of the Chedis, and Drupada and the king of Kasi and that mighty car-warrior Sikhandin' (list continues in pack excerpt).

statements.claim: It seemed the whole earth was moving with that one chariot, its sound rolling ahead like a promise toward the gates of Hastinapura.
statements.evidence: Figurative close to the departure scene; atmosphere rather than a factual assertion.

notes: Clean adaptation of MBh 5.083 (Ganguli). Every event, name and detail — rites, chariot, horses, Garuda, omens, sages, followers — maps directly to the passage. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira followed Krishna some distance on foot after the chariot set out and came up beside it to give his messages.
statements.evidence: Index summary: 'Yudhishthira, following Krishna some distance, asks him to salute and comfort his grieving mother Kunti...'; MBh 5.083: 'And while Krishna was proceeding, Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, followed him.'

statements.claim: The whole company — Bhima, Arjuna, the twins of Madri and the allied kings Chekitana, Dhrishtaketu, Drupada, the king of Kasi and Sikhandin — had come out with the chariot and fallen back one by one, until only the eldest Pandava remained walking after it.
statements.evidence: Pack confirms these figures followed the chariot (5.083 list); the 'fallen back one by one, only Yudhishthira left' staging is narrative arrangement to set up his private words, not contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: Yudhishthira asked Krishna to ask after Kunti's welfare, salute her, embrace her and comfort her over and over, for she was overwhelmed with grief on account of her sons.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'That lady who hath brought us from our infancy... should be asked about her welfare--Salute and embrace, and, oh, comfort her over and over, overwhelmed with grief as she is on account of her sons.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira sent salutations to the Kuru king Dhritarashtra, to Bhishma, to Drona, to Kripa, and to Vidura, 'endued with great wisdom'.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'Salute her for me, the Kuru king Dhritarashtra also... and Bhishma, and Drona, and Kripa... and also Vidura endued with great wisdom.'

statements.claim: Background glosses on the elders: Dhritarashtra the blind father who watched his son swallow a kingdom and did nothing; Bhishma who taught them arms and is bound to the other side by his vow; Drona and Kripa the teachers who shaped them; Vidura the wise uncle who stood by the Pandavas when no one else dared.
statements.evidence: Identifying character glosses attached to the pack-supported salutation list; canonical background framing rather than new sourceable claims, and nothing contradicts the pack.

statements.claim: Krishna took the messages into his keeping and promised each would be delivered exactly as given — the embrace for the mother, salutations for the king, honours for the elders, warm regard for Vidura.
statements.evidence: Krishna's accepting reply falls beyond the pack excerpt's cutoff; the promise is continuity narration consistent with his undertaking the errand. Index summary does not record Krishna's reply.

statements.claim: Nothing was asked for himself: Yudhishthira sent no demand, no warning and no word of his own rights — only his mother's grief and courtesy owed to the old.
statements.evidence: Non-factual framing summarizing the message content, which the pack excerpt bears out (greetings and salutations only).

statements.claim: Krishna also carried his own word to Arjuna: he would go to king Dhritarashtra desirous of accomplishing what is consistent with righteousness, what may be beneficial (to the Pandavas) and what is for the good of the Kurus.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: 'Yes, I will go to king Dhritarashtra, desirous of accomplishing what is consistent with righteousness, what may be beneficial to us, and what also is for the good of the Kurus.' (Story renders 'us' as 'the Pandavas', matching the speaker's party.)

statements.claim: Closing imagery: Yudhishthira watching the chariot shrink toward the horizon, the messages riding ahead 'like a small, careful map of everything the coming days might break'.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric close; interpretive commentary on the pack-supported parting scene.

notes: Supported by pack excerpt + index summary (MBh 5.083). Note: the pack's primary passage is truncated mid-list ('...the mighty car-warrior Sik'), so the message dialogue is carried by the verbatim excerpt and index. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Arjuna walked a few more steps beside the chariot and spoke again while the morning was still early and the chariot had not yet cleared the camp.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'Then Arjuna, proceeding a few steps, further said...' The early-morning setting matches 5.083's 'The night having passed away, a bright sun arose in the east.'

statements.claim: Recap of Arjuna's earlier plea: he had called Krishna the best friend of both houses, begged him to bring peace between the Pandavas and the sons of Dhritarashtra, and asked him to tell Suyodhana that refusing counsels fraught with virtue and profit would make him the victim of his own fate.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083 opening: Arjuna's full plea, including 'say unto our ever-wrathful brother Suyodhana... "If the foolish Duryodhana doth not accept thy auspicious and beneficial counsels fraught with virtue and profit, he will surely then be the victim of his fate."'

statements.claim: Arjuna's parting warning: 'If Dhritarashtra's son, who always adopts improper means, acts otherwise, then I shall surely, O Janardana, annihilate the whole race of the Kshatriyas.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'If, however, Dhritarashtra's son, who always adopts improper means, acts otherwise, then I shall surely, O Janardana, annihilate the Kshatriya race.'

statements.claim: Krishna had already accepted the errand, having answered that he would go to king Dhritarashtra desirous of righteousness, benefit and the good of the Kurus; the warning did not change the errand.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.083: Krishna's acceptance quote; the story's reading that the warning accompanies rather than alters the mission is sound framing.

statements.claim: Hearing this, Bhima set his feet on the earth and set forth a terrible shout.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): '...he set forth a terrible shout.' Index summary: 'Bhima, hearing this, sets forth a terrible shout that makes all bowmen tremble.'

statements.claim: The bowmen who heard the shout trembled, and the steeds and elephants lost all control of their bodies in fear.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'And hearing that shout of his, all the bowmen trembled in fear and steeds and elephants were seen to pass urine and excreta.' The story's 'lost all control of their bodies' is a decorous rendering of the same detail.

statements.claim: Atmosphere of the shout: some nearby felt the very ground tremble, the birds of omen that had followed the chariot scattered, and the camp fell silent after.
statements.evidence: Hyperbolic scene-setting extending the pack-supported terror of the shout; no independent sourceable fact, and nothing contradicts the pack.

statements.claim: Interpretive close: the shout was 'the war itself announcing its presence', and Duryodhana, when he chose, would be choosing in the hearing of that shout.
statements.evidence: Explicitly interpretive framing of the warning + roar, consistent with the pack's account of the mission's stakes.

notes: Clean. Arjuna's warning, the Bhima roar, and the bowmen/steeds/elephants reaction all match the pack excerpt verbatim (MBh 5.083). No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: On the road Krishna met a company of rishis blazing with Brahmic lustre, the radiance of men who had worn away worldly desires in austerity.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'on his way Kesava of mighty arms met with some Rishis blazing with Brahmic lustre.'

statements.claim: Krishna reined in, alighted from the chariot and went to worship the sages — as an envoy of kings he bows first before sages.
statements.evidence: Index summary: 'On the road Krishna alights to worship a band of celestial Rishis.' The envoy-bows-first clause is connective framing.

statements.claim: Among the sages Krishna recognised Narada, the tireless traveller of the three worlds, whose presence meant whatever happened there would be known everywhere.
statements.evidence: Pack index lists Narada among the story's characters (Krishna, Parashurama, Narada) for this event; Narada's role as celestial reporter is a canonical characterization. The character gloss is connective.

statements.claim: Parashurama, Jamadagni's son, came forward, approached Govinda the slayer of Madhu and embraced him.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083): 'Jamadagni's son... approached Govinda the slayer of Madhu, embraced him, and said...'

statements.claim: Parashurama said: 'We are desirous of beholding all the Kshatriyas of the earth assembled from every side... And we are anxious to listen to those words fraught with virtue and profit, which will be spoken by you unto the Kurus, in the presence of all.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.083) quotes these words near-verbatim (final clause clipped at the pack's truncation point).

statements.claim: The sages had renounced the world yet journeyed to hear Krishna's speech about peace; they would not take sides but came to witness where the fate of the earth would be spoken aloud.
statements.evidence: Interpretive gloss on the pack-quoted motive ('desirous of beholding all the Kshatriyas... anxious to listen to those words fraught with virtue and profit'), presented as the story's reading of the meeting.

statements.claim: Parashurama is described as the ancient sage feared by warriors since before the fathers of the men now gathering.
statements.evidence: Canonical background on Parashurama (the Kshatriya-destroying avatar) identifying him for readers; not stated in the pack excerpt but uncontradicted.

statements.claim: Krishna received the blessing and embrace, remounted the chariot and rolled on toward Hastinapura, leaving the rishis as witnesses behind him.
statements.evidence: Continuation consistent with the meeting occurring on Krishna's road to Hastinapura (pack: 'on his way'); the 'company of witnesses in the dust' imagery is connective close.

notes: Meeting, embrace and Parashurama's quoted words all match the pack excerpt (MBh 5.083); Narada's presence is supported by the pack's character index. Primary passage in the pack is truncated, so the excerpt + index carry the evidence. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: When Krishna set out from Upaplavya, ten mighty car-warriors capable of slaying hostile heroes, fully armed, rode behind his chariot, with a thousand foot-soldiers and a thousand horsemen and attendants by the hundred carrying provisions in abundance.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'ten mighty car-warriors, capable of slaying hostile heroes, fully armed, followed in his train. And a thousand foot-soldiers, and a thousand horsemen, and attendants by hundreds, also formed his train, carrying... provisions in abundance.'

statements.claim: Janamejaya, the king to whom the tale was told, asked how Krishna journeyed and what omens were seen at his setting out.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: Janamejaya asks 'How did the illustrious slayer of Madhu... proceed on his journey? And what omens were seen when that hero set out?'

statements.claim: Dread omens at Krishna's departure: thunder and lightning with no clouds, fleecy clouds raining in his rear, the seven great rivers (Sindhu among them) flowing backwards, reversed directions, fires blazing from the earth, repeated earth-tremors, wells and water-vessels swelling over, universal darkness and dust hiding the points of the horizon, and loud roars with no visible source.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084 narrates each omen near-verbatim: 'Though there were no clouds in the sky, yet the roll of thunder accompanied by flashes of lightning was heard... The seven large rivers including the Sindhu (Indus) though flowing eastwards then flowed in opposite directions... wells and water-vessels by hundreds swelled up and ran out... Loud roars were heard in the sky without any being being visible...'

statements.claim: A south-westerly wind, harsh with thunder, uprooting trees by the thousands, crushed the city of Hastinapura.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'A south-westerly wind, with the harsh rattle of the thunder, uprooting trees by the thousands, crushed the city of Hastinapura.'

statements.claim: In the places through which Krishna passed the world turned gentle: delicious breezes, showers of lotuses and fragrant flowers, a road free of prickly grass and thorns.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'In those places... through which he of Vrishni's race passed, delicious breezes blew and everything became auspicious. Showers of lotuses and fragrant flowers fell there. The very road became delightful, being free from prickly grass and thorns.'

statements.claim: Wherever he stayed, Brahmanas by the thousand glorified the giver of wealth and worshipped him with dishes of curds, ghee and honey and presents of wealth; women came out and strewed fragrant wild flowers on him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'Brahmanas by thousands glorified that giver of wealth... and worshipped him with dishes of curds, ghee, honey, and presents of wealth. The very women, coming out on the road, strewed wild flowers of great fragrance on the person of that illustrious hero.'

statements.claim: He passed villages abounding in bees and diverse cities and kingdoms and came to Salibhavana, filled with every kind of crop, delicious and sacred.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'He then came upon a delightful spot called Salibhavana which was filled with every kind of crops... after having... seen various villages abounding in bees... and after having passed through diverse cities and kingdoms.'

statements.claim: The cheerful citizens of Upaplavya, well-protected by the Bharatas and free from anxiety about invaders, came out of their town and stood on the way to behold Krishna, and worshipped him with all the honours of a guest.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'Always cheerful and of good hearts, well-protected by the Bharatas and therefore free from all anxieties on account of the designs of invaders... many of the citizens of Upaplavya, coming out of their town, stood together on the way, desirous of beholding Krishna... worshipped him... with all the honours of a guest.'

statements.claim: When Kesava came to Vrikasthala the sun reddened the sky with straggling rays; alighting, he performed purificatory rites, had the steeds unharnessed and said his evening prayers; Daruka tended the horses according to the rules of equine science, removing yokes and traces and letting them loose.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'the sun seemed to redden the sky by his straggling rays of light. Alighting from his car, he duly went through the usual purificatory rites, and ordering the steeds to be unharnessed, he set himself to say his evening prayers. And Daruka also, setting the steeds free, tended them according to the rules of equine science, and taking off the yokes and traces, let them loose.'

statements.claim: Krishna said, 'Here we must pass the night, for the sake of Yudhishthira's mission,' and the attendants raised a temporary abode and prepared excellent food and drink.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084: 'the slayer of Madhu said, "Here must we pass the night for the sake of Yudhishthira's mission."... the attendants soon set a temporary abode and prepared in a trice excellent food and drink.'

statements.claim: The noble, high-born, modest, Veda-obedient Brahmanas of the village honoured him with benedictions and auspicious speeches and placed their wealthy houses at his disposal; saying 'Enough', Krishna paid them homage each according to rank, went with them to their houses, returned in their company to his own tent, fed all the Brahmanas with sweetmeats and took his meals with them, passing the night happily.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.084 narrates the whole exchange, including 'Saying unto them--"Enough"--the illustrious Krishna paid them proper homage, each according to his rank... And feeding all the Brahmanas with sweet-meats and himself taking his meals with them, Kesava passed the night happily there.'

statements.claim: Closing line — Krishna passed the night 'at the threshold of the city whose sky had darkened at his coming'.
statements.evidence: Connective close recalling the pack-supported omens that crushed/darkened Hastinapura.

notes: Near-complete faithful rendering of MBh 5.084 (Ganguli): retinue, both omen catalogues (ruin for Hastinapura, auspiciousness on Krishna's route), Salibhavana, Upaplavya citizens, and the Vrikasthala night all match the passage. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Learning from his spies that the slayer of Madhu had set out, Dhritarashtra's hair stood on end; he addressed Bhishma, Drona, Sanjaya and Vidura, and spoke to Duryodhana and his counsellors about honouring Krishna.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085: 'understanding from his spies that the slayer of Madhu had set out, Dhritarashtra, with his hair standing erect, respectfully addressing the mighty-armed Bhishma and Drona and Sanjaya and the illustrious Vidura, said these words unto Duryodhana and his counsellors.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra's speech: men, women and children everywhere talk of Dasarha of great prowess coming for the Pandavas' sake; he is the Lord of all creatures on whom rests everything, full of intelligence, prowess, wisdom and energy, eternal Virtue itself, whose worship brings happiness and neglect misery.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085 quotes the speech near-verbatim ('strange and wonderful is the news that we hear... He is the Lord of all creatures, and on him resteth the course of every thing in the universe... eternal Virtue. If worshipped he is sure to bestow happiness; and if not worshipped he is sure to inflict misery.').

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra ordered pavilions furnished with every object of enjoyment set up on the road and asked what Bhishma thought; Bhishma and the others applauded the words, saying 'Excellent'.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085: 'Let pavilions be set up on the road, furnished with every object of enjoyment... What doth Bhishma think in this matter?' ... 'Bhishma and others, all applauding those words of king Dhritarashtra, said,--"Excellent."'

statements.claim: Duryodhana ordered delightful sites chosen for pavilions abounding with gems of every kind at proper intervals; he sent handsome seats, beautiful girls, scents and ornaments, fine robes, excellent viands, drinks of diverse qualities and fragrant garlands.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085: 'King Duryodhana then... ordered delightful sites to be chosen for the erection of pavilions. Many pavilions were thereupon constructed abounding with gems of every kind... And the king sent thither handsome seats... beautiful girls, and scents and ornaments, and fine robes, and excellent viands, and drink of diverse qualities, and fragrant garlands of many kinds.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana took especial care to erect a highly beautiful pavilion full of precious gems at Vrikasthala for Krishna's reception, and once the godlike arrangements (far above human capacity) were done, he informed Dhritarashtra.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085: 'the king of the Kurus took especial care to erect, for the reception of Krishna, a highly beautiful pavilion at Vrikasthala, full of precious gems. And having made all these arrangements that were god-like and much above the capacity of human beings... informed Dhritarashtra of the same.'

statements.claim: The road from Vrikasthala to the capital became a pageant; travellers and citizens slowed to look, and talk was all of the wealth being spent for one man.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric expansion of the pack-supported display; the specific bystander reactions are invented observers, not contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: Kesava arrived at the capital of the Kurus and passed all the gem-studded pavilions, seats, garlands and viands by without casting a single glance at them; no gem drew his eyes.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.085: 'Kesava, however, of Dasarha's race, arrived at the capital of the Kurus, without casting a single glance at all those pavilions and all those gems of diverse kinds.'

statements.claim: Interpretive close: Duryodhana built as though magnificence could dazzle Krishna into alliance, but Krishna, who needed nothing, made the whole architecture of the welcome irrelevant.
statements.evidence: Explicitly interpretive contrast of the lavish reception with Krishna's disregard; consistent with the pack, not asserted by it.

notes: Faithful rendering of MBh 5.085 (Ganguli) — Dhritarashtra's speech, the 'Excellent' response, Duryodhana's pavilions/gifts and the Vrikasthala pavilion, and Krishna passing all by without a glance are all in the passage. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Scene framing: Dhritarashtra, planning lavish gifts for Krishna, spoke of heaping wealth on him and most of the assembly took it for wisdom, until Vidura answered with the truth.
statements.evidence: Vidura's speech in the pack (5.087) presupposes Dhritarashtra's wish to give ('It is much, O king, that thou wishes to give unto Kesava as thy guest'); the assembly's reaction is connective staging. Dhritarashtra is blind — canonical epithet used throughout the corpus.

statements.claim: Vidura's opening: Dhritarashtra is respected by the three worlds, loved and regarded by everybody, and at his age can never speak against scripture or well-directed reason; virtue resides in him permanently like characters on stone, light in the sun, billows in the ocean.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'thou art respected by three worlds... Venerable in year as thou art, what thou wilt say at this age can never be against the dictates of the scriptures... virtue resideth in thee permanently' — with the same similes.

statements.claim: Vidura urged him to strive with friends and kinsmen to retain his virtues, adopt sincerity of behaviour, and not from folly cause the wholesale destruction of his sons, grandsons, friends, kinsmen and all that are dear to him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'Strive, therefore, with thy friends and kinsmen to retain those virtues of thine. Oh, adopt sincerity of behaviour. Do not from folly, cause a wholesale destruction of thy sons, grandsons, friends, kinsmen, and all that are dear to thee.'

statements.claim: Vidura said Kesava deserves all the offered gifts and much more — the whole earth itself — but swore by his own soul that Dhritarashtra did not wish to give them from virtue or to please Krishna: all of it betrays deception, falsehood and insincerity.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'Know, however, that Kesava deserves all this and much more, aye, the whole earth itself. I truly swear by my own soul that thou dost not wish to give all this unto Krishna either from motives of virtue or for the object of doing what is agreeable to him... all this betrays only deception, falsehood, and insincerity.'

statements.claim: Vidura exposed the secret purpose: the five Pandavas desire only five villages and Dhritarashtra will not give even that, so he is unwilling to make peace and seeks to win Krishna by wealth and separate Kesava from the Pandavas.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'By the external acts, O king, I know thy secret purpose. The five Pandavas, O king, desire only five villages. Thou, however, dost not wish to give them even that. Thou art, therefore, unwilling to make peace. Thou seekest to make the mighty-armed hero of Vrishni's race thy own by means of thy wealth... thou seekest to separate Kesava from the Pandavas.'

statements.claim: Vidura declared Dhritarashtra unable by wealth, attention or worship to separate Krishna from Dhananjaya, knowing Krishna's magnanimity, Arjuna's firm devotion, and that Dhananjaya, Kesava's very life, can never be given up.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'I tell thee, however, that thou art unable, by wealth, or attention, or worship, to separate Krishna from Dhananjaya. I know the magnanimity of Krishna; I know the firm devotion of Arjuna towards him, I know that Dhananjaya, who is Kesava's life, is incapable of being given up by the latter.'

statements.claim: Vidura said Janardana will accept nothing but a vessel of water, the washing of his feet and the usual enquiries after the welfare of those he will see; Dhritarashtra should offer the hospitality most agreeable to him, for no respect may not be offered to Janardana.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'Save only a vessel of water, save only the washing of his feet, save only the (usual) enquiries after the welfare (of those he will see), Janardana will not accept any other hospitality or set his eyes on any other thing... there is no respect that may not be offered to Janardana.'

statements.claim: Vidura urged the king to give Kesava the object he comes for — peace between Dhritarashtra and Duryodhana on one side and the Pandavas on the other — to follow his counsels and behave as a father toward the Pandavas, who are children to him in years and disposed to pay him filial regard.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.087: 'Give unto Kesava... that object in expectation of which... he cometh to the Kurus. Kesava desires peace to be established between thee and Duryodhana on one side and the Pandavas on the other... Thou art their father, O king, and the Pandavas are thy sons... behave as father towards them, that are disposed to pay thee filial regard.'

statements.claim: Interpretive close: the gifts were a strategy to prise Krishna loose from the Pandavas, the peace Krishna offered was real, and the question hanging over the hall was whether anyone would hear it.
statements.evidence: Summary reading of Vidura's speech, directly grounded in the pack-quoted content.

notes: Vidura's entire admonition is carried near-verbatim from MBh 5.087 (Ganguli); all named points — five villages, inability to separate Krishna from Dhananjaya, the water/feet-washing-only hospitality, the plea for peace — match. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: Duryodhana agreed with Vidura that all said about Krishna was truly said: Janardana is greatly devoted to the Pandavas and can never be separated from them.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'All that Vidura hath said about Krishna, hath indeed, been truly said; for Janardana is greatly devoted to the Pandavas and can never be separated from them.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana argued the proposed wealth ought never to be bestowed: Kesava is not unworthy of worship but time and place are against it, for he would think he was being worshipped out of fear, and an intelligent Kshatriya must not do what brings disgrace.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'All the diverse kinds of wealth... ought never to be bestowed upon him. Kesava is, of course, not unworthy of our worship, but both time and place are against it, for he... will very likely think that we are worshipping him out of fear... an intelligent Kshatriya must not do that which may bring disgrace upon him.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana concluded it was out of place to give Krishna anything now, for war having been decided upon should never be put off by hospitality — though the large-eyed Krishna deserves the most reverential worship of the three worlds.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'the large-eyed Krishna deserveth the most reverential worship of the three worlds. It is quite out of place, therefore... to give him anything now, for war having been decided upon, it should never be put off by hospitality.'

statements.claim: Bhishma answered: worshipped or not, Janardana never becomes angry; none can treat him with disrespect for he is not contemptible; whatever he purposes cannot be frustrated; so do without hesitation what Krishna says, bring about peace with the Pandavas through Vasudeva, and tell him only what is agreeable.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088 quotes Bhishma's reply to Duryodhana near-verbatim, including 'Do without hesitation what Krishna of mighty arms sayeth and bring about peace with the Pandavas through Vasudeva as the means.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana declared he could by no means live sharing his swelling prosperity with the Pandavas and formed a great resolution: to imprison Janardana, the refuge of the Pandavas, when he comes the next morning, so that the Vrishnis, the Pandavas and the whole earth would submit to him; he asked Bhishma for the means so Krishna would not guess the purpose.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'I will imprison Janardana who is the refuge of the Pandavas. He will come here tomorrow morning; and when he is confined, the Vrishnis and the Pandavas, aye, the whole earth, will submit to me. What may be the means for accomplishing it, so that Janardana may not guess our purpose... it behoveth thee to say.'

statements.claim: Hearing these fearful words about imprisoning Krishna, Dhritarashtra and all his counsellors were very much pained and deeply afflicted; the king protested that it is not immemorial custom — Hrishikesa comes as an ambassador, is related to them and dear to them, has done no wrong, and does not deserve imprisonment.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'Dhritarashtra, with all his counsellors, was very much pained and became deeply afflicted... "O ruler of men, never say this again, this is not immemorial custom. Hrishikesa cometh here as an ambassador. He is, besides, related to and is dear to us. He hath done us no wrong; how then doth he deserves imprisonment?"'

statements.claim: Bhishma denounced the plan: this wicked son's hour has come, he chooses evil though entreated by well-wishers, Dhritarashtra follows in the wake of a wicked wretch who treads a thorny path, and the wicked son with his counsellors, coming in contact with Krishna of unstained acts, will be destroyed in a moment; Bhishma declared he dared not listen to such words.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'This wicked son of thine... hath his hour come... will be destroyed in a moment. I dare not listen to the words of this sinful and wicked wretch that hath abandoned all virtue.'

statements.claim: Bhishma, inflamed with rage, rose and left the assembly.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.088: 'Having said this, that aged chief of the Bharata race, Bhishma of unbaffled prowess, inflamed with rage rose and left that place.'

statements.claim: Closing tableau — the assembly staring after him, the blind king stricken, the prince unmoved, and the plan to imprison the ambassador left standing in the hall like a storm not yet broken.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric close consistent with the pack; 'blind king' is the canonical epithet for Dhritarashtra used throughout the corpus.

notes: Faithful rendering of MBh 5.088 (Ganguli): Duryodhana's refusal of gifts, his imprison-Krishna resolution, Dhritarashtra's pained protest and Bhishma's denunciation and departure all match the passage near-verbatim and in order. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.
